questions.text: What is Henry's law ? Give one application of it.

answer.text:
Henry's law: the partial pressure of a gas above a solution is directly proportional to the mole fraction of the gas dissolved in the solution, i.e. $p = K_H\,x$, where $p$ = partial pressure of the gas, $x$ = its mole fraction in solution and $K_H$ = Henry's law constant.
Application (any one): to increase the solubility of $CO_2$ in soft drinks and soda water, the bottle is sealed under high pressure.

questions.text: The vapour pressure of pure liquid X and pure liquid Y at 25 °C are 120 mm Hg and 160 mm Hg respectively. If equal moles of X and Y are mixed to form an ideal solution, calculate the vapour pressure of the solution.

answer.text:
For an ideal binary solution, $p_{Total} = p^\circ_X\chi_X + p^\circ_Y\chi_Y$, with $\chi_X = \chi_Y = 0.5$.
$p_{Total} = (120 \times 0.5) + (160 \times 0.5) = 140\ \text{mm Hg}$.

questions.text: When $19{\cdot}5$ g of $F{-}CH_2{-}COOH$ (Molar mass $= 78$ g mol$^{-1}$), is dissolved in 500 g of water, the depression in freezing point is observed to be 1 °C. Calculate the degree of dissociation of $F{-}CH_2{-}COOH$. [Given : $K_f$ for water $= 1{\cdot}86$ K kg mol$^{-1}$]

answer.text:
$\Delta T_f = i\,K_f\,m = i\,K_f\,\dfrac{w_B}{M_B}\times\dfrac{1000}{w_A}$
$1 = i \times 1.86 \times \dfrac{19.5}{78}\times\dfrac{1000}{500}$, so $i = 1.075$.
Degree of dissociation $\alpha = \dfrac{i-1}{n-1} = \dfrac{1.075-1}{2-1} = 0.075$.

Calculate the percentage association of acid if it forms a dimer in the solution. [Given : $K_f$ for benzene $= 5{\cdot}12$ K kg mol$^{-1}$]

For association, $\alpha = \dfrac{1-i}{1-\frac{1}{n}} = \dfrac{1-0.527}{1-\frac{1}{2}} = 0.946$ (i.e. 94.6%).

questions.text: If benzoic acid (M $= 122$ g mol$^{-1}$) is associated into a dimer when dissolved in benzene and the osmotic pressure of a solution of $6{\cdot}1$ g of benzoic acid in 100 mL benzene is $6{\cdot}5$ atm at 27 °C, then what is the percentage association of benzoic acid ? (Given : R $= 0{\cdot}0821$ L atm K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$)

answer.text:
$\pi = i\dfrac{n_B}{V}RT = i\dfrac{w_B}{M_B}\times\dfrac{1000}{V}\times RT$
$6.5 = i \times \dfrac{6.1}{122}\times\dfrac{1000}{100}\times 0.0821 \times 300$, so $i = \dfrac{6.5\times122}{6.1\times0.0821\times300\times10} = 0.528$.
For association, $\alpha = \dfrac{1-i}{1-\frac{1}{n}} = \dfrac{1-0.528}{1-\frac{1}{2}} = 0.944$ (i.e. 94.4%).

questions.text: (i) Why is boiling point of 1M NaCl solution more than that of 1M glucose solution ? (ii) A non-volatile solute 'X' (molar mass $= 50$ g mol$^{-1}$) when dissolved in 78 g of benzene reduced its vapour pressure to 90%. Calculate the mass of X dissolved in the solution. (iii) Calculate the boiling point elevation for a solution prepared by adding 10 g of $MgCl_2$ to 200 g of water assuming $MgCl_2$ is completely dissociated. ($K_b$ for Water $= 0{\cdot}512$ K kg mol$^{-1}$, Molar mass $MgCl_2 = 95$ g mol$^{-1}$)
questions.topic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass

answer.text:
(a)(i) NaCl causes a greater colligative effect than glucose because NaCl dissociates, giving more particles in solution (its van't Hoff factor $i$ is greater than that of glucose).
(ii) Relative lowering of vapour pressure: $\dfrac{p^0 - p}{p^0} = x_2 = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1+n_2}$. With $p = 0.9\,p^0$ and $n_1 = \dfrac{78}{78} = 1$:
$\dfrac{p^0 - 0.9p^0}{p^0} = \dfrac{w/50}{(w/50)+1}$, giving $0.1\left(\dfrac{w}{50}+1\right) = \dfrac{w}{50}$, so $w = 5.55\ \text{g}$.
(iii) $\Delta T_b = i\,K_b\,m$ with $i = 3$: $\Delta T_b = 3 \times 0.512 \times \dfrac{10}{95}\times\dfrac{1000}{200} = 0.81\ \text{K (°C)}$.

questions.text: (i) Why is the value of Van't Hoff factor for ethanoic acid in benzene close to $0{\cdot}5$ ? (ii) Determine the osmotic pressure of a solution prepared by dissolving $2{\cdot}32 \times 10^{-2}$ g of $K_2SO_4$ in 2 L of solution at 25 °C, assuming $K_2SO_4$ is completely dissociated. (R $= 0{\cdot}082$ L atm K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$, Molar mass $K_2SO_4 = 174$ g mol$^{-1}$) (iii) When $25{\cdot}6$ g of Sulphur was dissolved in 1000 g of benzene, the freezing point lowered by $0{\cdot}512$ K. Calculate the formula of Sulphur ($S_x$). ($K_f$ for benzene $= 5{\cdot}12$ K kg mol$^{-1}$, Atomic mass of Sulphur $= 32$ g mol$^{-1}$)

answer.text:
(b)(i) The van't Hoff factor of ethanoic acid (in benzene) is about $0.5$ because ethanoic-acid molecules associate to form dimers, so the number of particles is nearly halved.
(ii) $\pi = i\,CRT$ with $i = 3$: $\pi = 3 \times \dfrac{2.32\times10^{-2}}{174\times2}\times 0.082 \times 298 = 4.88\times10^{-3}\ \text{atm}$.
(iii) $\Delta T_b = K_f\,\dfrac{w_2}{M_2}\times\dfrac{1000}{w_1}$: $0.512 = 5.12 \times \dfrac{25.6}{M_2}\times\dfrac{1000}{1000}$, so $M_2 = 256$. Since $S \times x = 256$ and $S = 32$, $x = \dfrac{256}{32} = 8$, i.e. the molecular formula is $S_8$.

questions.text: (i) At the same temperature, $CO_2$ gas is more soluble in water than $O_2$ gas. Which one of them will have higher value of $K_H$ and why ? (ii) How does the size of blood cells change when placed in an aqueous solution containing more than $0{\cdot}9\%$ (mass/volume) sodium chloride ? (iii) 1 molal aqueous solution of an electrolyte $A_2B_3$ is 60% ionized. Calculate the boiling point of the solution. (Given : $K_b$ for $H_2O = 0{\cdot}52$ K kg mol$^{-1}$)
questions.topic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass

answer.text:
(a)(i) Since $K_H \propto \dfrac{1}{\text{solubility}}$ of the gas, $O_2$ has the higher $K_H$ value (the higher the $K_H$, the lower the solubility of the gas in the liquid).
(ii) The blood cells shrink (in a hypertonic solution, due to exosmosis).
(iii) $\Delta T_b = i\,K_b\,m$. First find i from $\alpha = \dfrac{i-1}{n-1}$ with $n = 5$: $0.6 = \dfrac{i-1}{5-1} \Rightarrow i = 3.4$.
$\Delta T_b = 3.4 \times 0.52 \times 1 = 1.768\ \text{K}$, so $T_b = 373 + 1.768 = 374.768\ \text{K}$.

Which colligative property is preferred for the molar mass determination of macromolecules ? (iii) Why are equimolar solutions of sodium chloride and glucose not isotonic ?

answer.text:
(b)(i) $P_T = p_A^0 x_A + p_B^0 x_B = (75\times0.4) + (25\times0.6) = 30 + 15 = 45\ \text{mm Hg}$.
In the vapour phase, $y_B = \dfrac{p_B}{P_T} = \dfrac{p_B^0 x_B}{P_T} = \dfrac{15}{45} = \dfrac{1}{3} = 0.33$.
(ii) A colligative property depends on the number of solute particles, not on the nature of the solute; e.g. osmotic pressure. NaCl gives a greater effect than glucose because NaCl dissociates ($i = 2$) whereas glucose does not ($i = 1$) — from $\pi = iCRT$.

questions.text: The vapour pressure of a solvent at 283 K is 100 mm Hg. Calculate the vapour pressure of a dilute solution containing 1 mole of a strong electrolyte AB in 50 moles of the solvent at 283 K (assuming complete dissociation of solute AB).

answer.text:
$\dfrac{p^0 - p_s}{p^0} = i\times\chi$. For $AB \rightarrow A^+ + B^-$, $i = 2$.
For a dilute solution, $\dfrac{100 - p_s}{100} = 2\times\dfrac{n_{AB}}{n_{solvent}} = 2\times\dfrac{1}{50}$, so $100 - p_s = 4$, i.e. $p_s = 96\ \text{mm Hg}$.

questions.text: The spontaneous flow of the solvent through a semipermeable membrane from a pure solvent to a solution or from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution is called osmosis. The phenomenon of osmosis can be demonstrated by taking two eggs of the same size. In an egg, the membrane below the shell and around the egg material is semipermeable. The outer hard shell can be removed by putting the egg in dilute hydrochloric acid. After removing the hard shell, one egg is placed in distilled water and the other in a saturated salt solution. After some time, the egg placed in distilled water swells-up while the egg placed in salt solution shrinks. The external pressure applied to stop the osmosis is termed as osmotic pressure (a colligative property). Reverse osmosis takes place when the applied external pressure becomes larger than the osmotic pressure. (a) Define reverse osmosis. Name one SPM which can be used in the process of reverse osmosis. (b) (i) What do you expect to happen when red blood corpuscles (RBC's) are placed in 0$\cdot$5% NaC$l$ solution ? OR (b) (ii) Which one of the following will have higher osmotic pressure in 1 M KC$l$ or 1 M urea solution. Justify your answer. (c) Why osmotic pressure is a colligative property ?
questions.topic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass

answer.text:
(a) Reverse osmosis: when the external pressure applied to the solution is larger than the osmotic pressure, the solvent moves from the solution to the solvent side through the semipermeable membrane (the direction of osmosis is reversed). questions.text: According to the generally accepted definition of the ideal solution there are equal interaction forces acting between molecules belonging to the same or different species. (This is equivalent to the statement that the activity of the components equals the concentration.) Strictly speaking, this condition is fulfilled only in exceptional cases for mixtures (optical isomers, isotopic mixtures of an element, hydrocarbon mixtures). It is still usual to talk about ideal solutions as limiting cases in reality since very dilute solutions behave ideally with respect to the solvent. This view is further supported by the fact that Raoult's law empirically found for describing the behaviour of the solvent in dilute solutions can be deduced thermodynamically via the assumption of ideal behaviour of the solvent. (a) Give one example of miscible liquid pair which shows negative deviation from Raoult's law. What is the reason for such deviation ? (b) (i) State Raoult's law for a solution containing volatile components. OR (b) (ii) Raoult's law is a special case of Henry's law. Comment. (c) Write two characteristics of an ideal solution.

answer.text:
(a) Chloroform and acetone (or any other correct example) — the A–B interactions are stronger than the A–A and B–B interactions (negative deviation).
(b)(i) Raoult's law: for a solution, the partial vapour pressure of each volatile component is directly proportional to its mole fraction.
(c) Characteristics of an ideal solution (any two): the enthalpy of mixing is zero ($\Delta_{mix}H = 0$); the volume of mixing is zero ($\Delta_{mix}V = 0$).
OR (b)(ii) Henry's law and Raoult's law become identical when the pure-component vapour pressure equals the Henry constant: $p = p^0\chi$ and $p = K_H\chi$, so when $p^0 = K_H$, $p \propto \chi$ for both laws.

questions.text: Calculate the boiling point of a solution containing $0{\cdot}61$ g of benzoic acid (Molar mass $= 122$ g mol$^{-1}$) in 5 g of $CS_2$ in which it dimerises to the extent of 88%. answer.text:
Given degree of association $\alpha = 88\% = 0.88$ (the solute dimerises, $n = 2$). For association, $\alpha = \dfrac{1-i}{1-\frac{1}{n}}$, so
$0.88 = \dfrac{1-i}{1-\frac{1}{2}} \Rightarrow i = 0.56$.
Elevation of boiling point $\Delta T_b = i\,K_b\,\dfrac{W_B}{M_B}\times\dfrac{1000}{W_A} = 0.56\times2.3\times\dfrac{0.61}{122}\times\dfrac{1000}{5} = 1.288\ \text{K}$.

$0.70 = 2.52\times\dfrac{1.5}{M_B}\times\dfrac{1000}{90}$

questions.text: Osmosis is a process by which the molecules of a solvent pass from a solution of low solute concentration to a solution of high solute concentration through a semi-permeable membrane. Osmotic pressure is a colligative property. When the applied pressure on a solution exceeds its osmotic pressure, reverse osmosis occurs. When two solutions are separated by a semipermeable membrane and they have same osmotic pressure they are said to be isotonic. Of the two solutions separated by a semipermeable membrane, if one is a lower osmotic pressure, it is said to be hypotonic relative to the second solution. If it has a higher osmotic pressure, than the second solution, it is said to be hypertonic relative to the second solution. The osmotic pressure associated with the fluid inside the blood cell is equivalent to that of 0$\cdot$9% (mass/volume) sodium chloride solution called normal saline solution and it is safe to inject intravenously. Osmotic pressure is vital in daily life and nature. It helps in explain, why IV fluids match blood's osmotic pressure, its also the principle behind food preservation using salt or sugar. (a) Calculate the amount of $CaCl_2$ (i $= 2{\cdot}59$) dissolved in $2{\cdot}46$ litre of water such that its osmotic pressure is $0{\cdot}70$ atm at 27 $^\circ$C. [Given : R $= 0{\cdot}082$ L atm K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$, molar mass of $CaCl_2 = 111$ g mol$^{-1}$] (b) When raisins are kept in water, they get swollen. Name the phenomenon involved in this process. OR (b) Why osmotic pressure is more advantageous than other colligative properties ? (c) Which phenomenon is responsible for desalination of sea water ?

answer.text:
(a) Osmotic pressure $\Pi = iCRT = i\times\dfrac{W_B}{M_B}\times\dfrac{1}{V}RT$:
$0.70 = 2.59\times\dfrac{W_B}{111}\times\dfrac{1}{2.46}\times0.082\times300$
$W_B = \dfrac{0.70\times111\times2.46}{2.59\times0.082\times300} = 3\ \text{g}$.
(b) The phenomenon is osmosis.
OR (b) Osmotic pressure is preferred (over other colligative properties) for measuring molar masses because its magnitude is large even for very dilute solutions, it is measured at room temperature, and molarity (not molality) is used.
(c) The process used to purify sea water is reverse osmosis.

questions.text: Rahul set-up an experiment to find resistance of aqueous KCl solution for different concentrations at 298 K using a conductivity cell connected to a Wheatstone bridge. He fed the Wheatstone bridge with a.c. power in the audio frequency range 550 to 5000 cycles per second. Once the resistance was calculated from each half he also calculated the conductivity K and molar conductivity $\Lambda_m$ and recorded his readings in tabular form. Answer the following questions : (a) Why does conductivity decrease with dilution ? (b) If $\Lambda^\circ_m = 150{\cdot}0$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$, calculate the degree of dissociation of $0{\cdot}01$ M KCl. (c) If Rahul had used NaCl instead of KCl, would you expect the $\Lambda_m$ values to be more or less than those for KCl for a given concentration ? Justify. OR (c) Amit, a classmate of Rahul repeated the same experiment with $CH_3COOH$ solution instead of KCl solution. Give one point that would be similar and one that would be different in his observations as compared to Rahul.

answer.text:
(a) On dilution the molar conductivity increases because, although the number of ions per unit volume decreases, the ions move more freely (and for a weak electrolyte more of it dissociates).
(b) $\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^\circ} = \dfrac{141}{150} = 0.94$.
(c) $H^+$ conducts more because the mobility of $H^+$ is greater than that of $K^+$.
OR (c) Similarity: for both electrolytes $\Lambda_m$ increases on dilution.
Difference: for KCl (a strong electrolyte) $\Lambda_m$ increases gradually and $\Lambda_m^\circ$ can be obtained by extrapolating $\Lambda_m$ to zero concentration; whereas for $CH_3COOH$ (a weak electrolyte) $\Lambda_m$ increases steeply on dilution and $\Lambda_m^\circ$ cannot be obtained by extrapolation.

questions.text: Batteries and fuel cells are very useful forms of galvanic cell. Any battery or cell that we use as a source of electrical energy is basically a galvanic cell. However, for a battery to be of practical use it should be reasonably light, compact and its voltage should not vary appreciably during its use. There are mainly two types of batteries — primary batteries and secondary batteries. In the primary batteries, the reaction occurs only once and after use over a period of time the battery becomes dead and cannot be reused again, whereas the secondary batteries are rechargeable. Production of electricity by thermal plants is not a very efficient method and is a major source of pollution. To solve this problem, galvanic cells are designed in such a way that energy of combustion of fuels is directly converted into electrical energy, and these are known as fuel cells. One such fuel cell was used in the Apollo space programme. Answer the following questions : (a) How do primary batteries differ from secondary batteries ? (b) The cell potential of Mercury cell is $1{\cdot}35$ V, and remains constant during its life. Give reason. (c) Write the reactions involved in the recharging of the lead storage battery. OR (c) Write two advantages of fuel cells over other galvanic cells.

answer.text:
(a) Primary batteries are not rechargeable, whereas secondary batteries are rechargeable.
(b) In a fuel cell the e.m.f. does not change with use because the overall reaction does not involve any ion in solution whose concentration can change during its lifetime.
(c) Electrode reactions of the lead storage battery (on recharging):
Cathode: $PbSO_4(s) + 2e^- \rightarrow Pb(s) + SO_4^{2-}(aq)$.
Anode: $PbSO_4(s) + 2H_2O(l) \rightarrow PbO_2(s) + SO_4^{2-}(aq) + 4H^+(aq) + 2e^-$.
OR (c) Advantages of a fuel cell (any two): (i) more efficient; (ii) pollution-free.

In a galvanic cell, chemical energy of a redox reaction is converted into electrical energy, whereas in an electrolytic cell the redox reaction occurs on passing electricity. The simplest galvanic cell is one in which Zn rod is placed in a solution of $ZnSO_4$ and Cu rod is placed in a solution of $CuSO_4$. The two rods are connected by a metallic wire through a voltmeter. The two solutions are joined by a salt bridge. The difference between the two electrode potentials of the two electrodes is known as electromotive force. In the process of electrolysis, the decomposition of a substance takes place by passing an electric current. One mole of electric charge when passed through a cell will discharge half a mole of a divalent metal ion such as $Cu^{2+}$. This was first formulated by Faraday in the form of laws of electrolysis. Answer the following questions : (a) What is the function of a salt bridge in a galvanic cell ? (b) When does galvanic cell behave like an electrolytic cell ? (c) Can copper sulphate solution be stored in a pot made of zinc ? Explain with the help of the value of E° cell. ($E^\circ Cu^{2+}/Cu = 0{\cdot}34$ V) ($E^\circ Zn^{2+}/Zn = -0{\cdot}76$ V) OR (c) How much charge in terms of Faraday is required for the following : (i) 1 mol of $MnO_4^-$ to $Mn^{2+}$ (ii) 1 mol of $H_2O$ to $O_2$

answer.text:
(a) A salt bridge allows the flow of ions and completes the circuit / it maintains the electrical neutrality of the two half-cells.
(b) An external EMF greater than the cell EMF ($E_{ext} > E_{cell}$) is applied (to recharge the cell / to drive electrolysis).
(c) $E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{Cu^{2+}/Cu} - E^\circ_{Zn^{2+}/Zn} = 0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10\ \text{V}$. Since $E^\circ_{cell}$ is positive, the reaction takes place, so copper sulphate cannot be stored in a zinc vessel.
OR (c)(i) 5 F. (ii) 2 F.

Predict whether the reaction will be spontaneous or not at 25 $^\circ$C. [1 F $= 96500$ C mol$^{-1}$] (b) Tarnished silver contains $Ag_2S$. Can this tarnish be removed by placing tarnished silverware in an aluminium pan containing an inert electrolytic solution such as NaC$l$ ? The standard electrode potential for half reaction : $Ag_2S(s) + 2e^- \longrightarrow 2Ag(s) + S^{2-}$ is $-0{\cdot}71$ V and for $Al^{3+} + 3e^- \longrightarrow Al(s)$ is $-1{\cdot}66$ V.

(b) Yes, the tarnish can be removed. Aluminium has a more negative standard electrode potential than silver, so it reduces silver sulphide back to silver: $3\,Ag^+ + Al \rightarrow 3\,Ag + Al^{3+}$; $E^\circ_{cell} = -0.71 - (-1.66) = 0.95\ \text{V}$ (positive), so the reaction is feasible and the tarnish is removed.

answer.text:
(b)(i) Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions: the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte can be represented as the sum of the individual contributions of the anion and the cation of the electrolyte. It is used to determine (1) the limiting molar conductivity of a weak electrolyte, and (2) the dissociation constant of a weak electrolyte (or any other two suitable applications).

questions.text: State Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions. With the help of a curve, explain why it is not easy to determine $\Lambda_m^\circ$ for weak electrolytes by extrapolating the concentration $-$ molar conductivity curve, as it is for strong electrolytes.

answer.text:
The limiting (molar) conductivity $\Lambda^\circ_m$ of an electrolyte is equal to the sum of the individual contributions of its cation and anion (Kohlrausch's law).
In a plot of $\Lambda_m$ against $\sqrt{C}$, a strong electrolyte gives a nearly straight line that can be extrapolated to $\sqrt{C}\to0$ to give $\Lambda^\circ_m$ directly. For a weak electrolyte the curve rises steeply near zero concentration and, on extrapolation, runs almost parallel to the $\Lambda_m$-axis, so it does not give a definite intercept — hence $\Lambda^\circ_m$ of a weak electrolyte cannot be found this way (it is obtained using Kohlrausch's law instead).

(c) Why are magnesium blocks fixed to the iron pipelines carrying water ?

answer.text:

Electrochemistry is the study of the relationship between chemical energy and electrical energy. Many spontaneously occurring chemical reactions liberate electrical energy. In electrolysis, electrical energy is converted directly into chemical energy. The product of an electrolytic reaction depends on the nature of the material being electrolysed and the type of electrode used. Oxidising and reducing species present in the electrolytic cell and their standard electrode potential too, affect the products of electrolysis. Electrolysis plays an important role in most people's daily lives, whether it is for the manufacturing of aluminium, electroplating of metals, or the synthesis of chemical compounds. Michael Faraday was the first scientist who proposed two laws to explain the quantitative aspects of electrolysis, popularly known as Faraday's laws of electrolysis. (a) Predict the products of electrolysis in each of the following : (i) An aqueous solution of $CuCl_2$ with platinum electrodes. (ii) A concentrated solution of $H_2SO_4$ with platinum electrodes. (b) (i) How much charge in faraday is required for the reduction of 1 mol of $Ag^+$ to Ag ? OR (b) (ii) State Faraday's second law of electrolysis. (c) The following reactions occur at the anode during the electrolysis of aqueous sodium chloride solution : $Cl^-(aq) \to \tfrac{1}{2}Cl_2(g) + e^-$, $E^\circ_{cell} = 1{\cdot}36$ V (I); $2H_2O(l) \to O_2(g) + 4H^+(aq) + 4e^-$, $E^\circ_{cell} = 1{\cdot}23$ V (II). Which reaction is feasible at the anode and why ?

answer.text:
(a)(i) On electrolysis (of aqueous $CuCl_2$):
Anode: chlorine is liberated, $2Cl^- \longrightarrow Cl_2 + 2e^-$;
Cathode: copper is deposited, $Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \longrightarrow Cu$.
(ii) On electrolysis of a concentrated sulphate solution:
Anode: peroxodisulphate ion, $2SO_4^{2-} \longrightarrow S_2O_8^{2-} + 2e^-$;
Cathode: hydrogen, $H_2O + e^- \longrightarrow \tfrac{1}{2}H_2(g) + OH^-$.
(b)(i) The quantity of charge required is 1 Faraday.
OR (b)(ii) Faraday's second law of electrolysis: the amounts of different substances liberated by the same quantity of electricity passing through the electrolytic solution are proportional to their chemical equivalent weights.
(c) Reaction (I) is feasible; oxygen is not evolved (its expected reaction is suppressed) because of the overpotential of oxygen.

questions.text: A chemical reaction $2N_2O_5(g) \longrightarrow 4NO_2(g) + O_2(g)$ in gas phase was carried out in a closed vessel. The concentration of $NO_2$ was found to increase by $5 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$ in 10 seconds. Calculate : (a) the rate of formation of $NO_2$, and (b) the rate of consumption of $N_2O_5$.

answer.text:
For $2\,N_2O_5 \to 4\,NO_2 + O_2$:
$-\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\Delta[N_2O_5]}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{1}{4}\dfrac{\Delta[NO_2]}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{\Delta[O_2]}{\Delta t}$
(a) Rate of formation of $NO_2$: $\dfrac{1}{4}\dfrac{\Delta[NO_2]}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{1}{4}\times\dfrac{5\times10^{-3}}{10} = 1.25\times10^{-4}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$.
(b) Rate of disappearance of $N_2O_5$: $-\dfrac{\Delta[N_2O_5]}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{2}{4}\dfrac{\Delta[NO_2]}{\Delta t} = 0.5\times1.25\times10^{-4} = 0.625\times10^{-4} \ (= 6.25\times10^{-5})\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$.

(a) Order w.r.t. NO = 2; order w.r.t. $Br_2$ = 1.

questions.text: The rate of a chemical reaction is expressed either in terms of decrease in the concentration of reactants or increase in the concentration of a product per unit time. Rate of the reaction depends upon the nature of reactants, concentration of reactants, temperature, presence of catalyst, surface area of the reactants and presence of light. Rate of reaction is directly related to the concentration of reactant. Rate law states that the rate of reaction depends upon the concentration terms on which the rate of reaction actually depends, as observed experimentally. The sum of powers of the concentration of the reactants in the Rate law expression is called order of reaction while the number of reacting species taking part in an elementary reaction which must collide simultaneously in order to bring about a chemical reaction is called molecularity of the reaction. Answer the following questions : (a) (i) What is a rate determining step ? (ii) Define complex reaction. (b) What is the effect of temperature on the rate constant of a reaction ? OR (b) Why is molecularity applicable only for elementary reactions whereas order is applicable for elementary as well as complex reactions ? (c) The conversion of molecule X to Y follows second order kinetics. If concentration of X is increased 3 times, how will it affect the rate of formation of Y ?

answer.text:
(a)(i) The rate-determining step is the slowest step of the mechanism.
(ii) A complex reaction is a series of elementary reactions (a reaction involving two or more steps).
(b) The rate constant increases with an increase in temperature.
(c) The rate becomes 9 times (for a second-order dependence, tripling the concentration gives $3^2 = 9$).
OR (b) Molecularity is defined only for elementary reactions, whereas order is determined experimentally and so is applicable to both. (The molecularity of each elementary step in a complex reaction may differ, so it is meaningless for the overall reaction, whereas the order of a complex reaction is fixed by its slowest step.)

questions.text: Transition metals have incomplete d-subshell either in neutral atom or in their ions. The presence of partly filled d-orbitals in their atoms makes transition elements different from that of the non-transition elements. With partly filled d-orbitals, these elements exhibit certain characteristic properties such as display of a variety of oxidation states, formation of coloured ions and entering into complex formation with a variety of ligands. The transition metals and their compounds also exhibit catalytic properties and paramagnetic behaviour. The transition metals are very hard and have low volatility. An examination of the $E^\circ_{M^{2+}/M}$ values shows the varying trends : (a) On what basis can we say that Cu is a transition element but Zn is not ? (Atomic number : Cu $= 29$, Zn $= 30$) (b) Why do transition elements show variety of oxidation states ? (c) (i) Why do $E^\circ_{M^{2+}/M}$ values show irregular trend from Vanadium to Zinc ? (ii) How is the variability in oxidation states of transition metals different from that of the non-transition elements ? OR (c) (i) Of the $d^4$ species, $Cr^{2+}$ is strongly reducing while $Mn^{3+}$ is strongly oxidizing. Why ? answer.text:
(a) $Cu^{2+}$ is coloured whereas $Zn^{2+}$ is colourless because Cu has an incomplete d-orbital in the +2 state, whereas Zn has a fully filled d-orbital in both the ground state and the +2 state.
(b) Transition metals show variable oxidation states because both the (n–1)d and ns electrons take part in bond formation (due to their comparable energies) / due to the presence of unpaired d-electrons.
(c)(i) Because of the irregular values of the ionisation enthalpies ($\Delta_iH_1 + \Delta_iH_2$) and the sublimation enthalpies.
(ii) In transition metals the oxidation states differ by 1, whereas in non-transition metals they differ by 2.
OR (c)(i) $Cr^{2+}$ is a reducing agent because $Cr^{2+} \to Cr^{3+}$ attains the more stable half-filled $t_{2g}^3$ configuration; whereas $Mn^{3+}$ is an oxidising agent because $Mn^{3+} \to Mn^{2+}$ attains the more stable half-filled $d^5$ configuration.

questions.text: The involvement of $(n-1)$d electrons in the behaviour of transition elements impart certain distinct characteristics to these elements. Thus, in addition to variable oxidation states, they exhibit paramagnetic behaviour, catalytic properties and tendency for the formation of coloured ions. The transition metals react with a number of non-metals like oxygen, nitrogen and halogens. $KMnO_4$ and $K_2Cr_2O_7$ are common examples. The two series of inner transition elements, lanthanoids and actinoids, constitute the f-block of the periodic table. In the lanthanoids, there is regular decrease in atomic size with increase in atomic number due to the imperfect shielding effect of 4f-orbital electrons which causes contraction. Answer the following questions : (a) Why do transition metals and their compounds act as good catalysts ? (b) What is the cause of contraction in the atomic size of lanthanoids ? (c) Define lanthanoid contraction. How does it affect the atomic radii of the third transition series and the second transition series ? OR (c) In aqueous media, which is a stronger reducing agent — $Cr^{2+}$ or $Fe^{2+}$ and why ?

answer.text:
(a) Transition metals are good catalysts due to their ability to show multiple oxidation states and to form complexes / to provide a large surface area.
(b) Because of the poor shielding effect of the 4f orbitals (giving the lanthanoid contraction).
(c) Lanthanoid contraction: the overall (steady) decrease in atomic and ionic radii from La to Lu. Consequence: the atomic radii of the second and third transition series are very similar.
OR (c) $Cr^{2+}$ is a stronger reducing agent than $Fe^{2+}$. Reason: $Cr^{2+} \to Cr^{3+}$ involves $d^4 \to d^3$, whereas $Fe^{2+} \to Fe^{3+}$ involves $d^6 \to d^5$; in an aqueous medium the $d^3$ configuration is more stable than $d^5$.

(a) Zn has a fully filled d-orbital configuration in both the ground state and its oxidised (+2) state (so it is not a typical transition metal).
(b) The filling of the 4f orbital before the 5d orbital results in a steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii with increasing atomic number (lanthanoid contraction).

answer.text:
(b)(i) Lanthanoid contraction — the gradual decrease in the atomic (and ionic) radii of the lanthanoids from left to right, because the 4f orbitals (filled before the 5d) shield the nuclear charge poorly, giving a steady decrease in radius.
(ii) Transition-metal ions are coloured because of d--d transitions (due to the presence of unpaired d-electrons).
(iii) $Mn^{2+}$ has a half-filled ($3d^5$) configuration and $Zn^{2+}$ has a fully-filled ($3d^{10}$) configuration, so both are extra stable.
(iv) $Cu^{2+}$ is more stable (in water) because of its high hydration enthalpy $\Delta_{hyd}H^\circ$.

questions.text: Which of the following is the most stable complex species ?

Coordination compounds are widely present in the minerals, plant and animal worlds and are known to play many important functions in the area of analytical chemistry, metallurgy, biological systems and medicine. Alfred Werner's theory postulated the use of two types of linkages (primary and secondary), by a metal atom/ion in a coordination compound. He predicted the geometrical shapes of a large number of coordination entities using the property of isomerism. The Valence Bond Theory (VBT) explains the formation, magnetic behaviour and geometrical shapes of coordination compounds. It, however, fails to describe the optical properties of these compounds. The Crystal Field Theory (CFT) explains the effect of different crystal fields (provided by the ligands taken as point charges) on the degeneracy of d-orbital energies of the central metal atom/ion. Answer the following questions : (i) When a coordination compound $NiCl_2 \cdot 6H_2O$ is mixed with $AgNO_3$ solution, 2 moles of AgCl are precipitated per mole of the compound. Write the structural formula of the complex and secondary valency for Nickel ion. (ii) Write the IUPAC name of the ionisation isomer of $[Co(NH_3)_5(SO_4)]Cl$. (iii) Using Valence Bond Theory, predict the geometry and magnetic nature of : (1) $[Ni(CO)_4]$ (2) $[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}$ [Atomic number : Ni $= 28$, Fe $= 26$] OR (iii) Give reasons : (1) Low spin tetrahedral complexes are not formed. (2) $[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}$ is an inner orbital complex whereas $[Ni(NH_3)_6]^{2+}$ is an outer orbital complex. [Atomic number : Co $= 27$, Ni $= 28$]

answer.text:
(i) $[Ni(H_2O)_6]Cl_2$; coordination number = 6.
(ii) Pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) sulphate.
(iii)(1) $[Ni(CO)_4]$ — tetrahedral, diamagnetic. (2) $[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}$ — octahedral, paramagnetic.
OR (iii)(1) In $[NiCl_4]^{2-}$, $\Delta_t$ (the crystal-field splitting energy, CFSE) is not sufficient to pair the electrons.
(2) $NH_3$, being a strong-field ligand, can pair up the electrons to form $d^2sp^3$; but in $Ni^{2+}$ two vacant (inner) d-orbitals are not available, so $sp^3d^2$ is formed instead.

questions.text: Answer any three of the following questions : (a) Explain the type of hybridization in $[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}$ on the basis of valence bond theory. (Given : Atomic number of Fe $= 26$) (b) Draw the geometrical isomers of $[PtCl_2(en)_2]^{2+}$ ion. (c) $[NiCl_4]^{2-}$ is paramagnetic while $[Ni(CO)_4]$ is diamagnetic though both are tetrahedral. Why ? (d) Name the type of isomerism when ambidentate ligands are attached to central metal ion. Give one example of ambidentate ligand.

answer.text:
(a) $Fe = 3d^6 4s^2$, so $Fe^{3+} = 3d^5$. In $[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}$, $CN^-$ (a strong-field ligand) pairs the d-electrons, leaving two inner d-orbitals vacant; hence the hybridisation is $d^2sp^3$ (octahedral).
(b) $[Pt(en)_2Cl_2]^{2+}$ shows cis–trans (geometrical) isomerism: in the cis isomer the two $Cl$ ligands are adjacent, and in the trans isomer they are opposite.
(c) $Cl^-$, being a weak-field ligand, does not cause pairing, so $[NiCl_4]^{2-}$ is paramagnetic; whereas CO, being a strong-field ligand, causes pairing, so $[Ni(CO)_4]$ is diamagnetic.
(d) Linkage isomerism. Example: ambidentate ligands such as $CN^-$ / $NO_2^-$ / $SCN^-$.

questions.text: The Valence Bond Theory (VBT) explains the formation, magnetic behaviour and geometrical shapes of coordination compounds whereas 'The Crystal Field Theory' for coordination compounds is based on the effect of different crystal fields (provided by ligands taken as point charges), on the degeneracy of d-orbital energies of the central metal atom/ion. The splitting of the d-orbitals provides different electronic arrangements in strong and weak crystal fields. The crystal field theory attributes the colour of the coordination compounds to d-d transition of the electron. Coordination compounds find extensive applications in metallurgical processes, analytical and medicinal chemistry. Answer the following questions : (a) What is crystal field splitting energy ? (b) Give reason for the violet colour of the complex $[Ti(H_2O)_6]^{3+}$ on the basis of crystal field theory. (c) $[Cr(NH_3)_6]^{3+}$ is paramagnetic while $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$ is diamagnetic. Explain why. [Atomic No. : Cr $= 24$, Ni $= 28$] OR (c) Explain why $[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}$ is an inner orbital complex, whereas $[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{3+}$ is an outer orbital complex. [Atomic No. : Fe $= 26$]

answer.text:
(a) Crystal-field splitting energy: the energy involved in the splitting of the degenerate d-orbitals due to the presence of ligands in a definite geometry.
(b) $Ti^{3+} = 3d^1$ (i.e. $t_{2g}^1 e_g^0$); it is coloured due to d–d transition.
(c) $Cr^{3+} = 3d^3$ ($t_{2g}^3$): paramagnetic, due to three unpaired electrons (stable $t_{2g}^3$). $Ni^{2+} = 3d^8$: in $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$, $CN^-$ (a strong-field ligand) pairs up the electrons, so the complex is diamagnetic.
OR (c) $CN^-$, being a strong-field ligand, causes pairing of electrons in $[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}$, giving $d^2sp^3$ hybridisation (an inner-orbital complex using (n–1)d orbitals); whereas $H_2O$, being a weak-field ligand, does not cause pairing in $[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{3+}$, giving $sp^3d^2$ hybridisation (an outer-orbital complex using nd orbitals).

questions.text: The nature of bonding, structure of the coordination compound can be explained to some extent by valence bond theory. The central metal atom/ion makes available a number of vacant orbitals equal to its coordination number. The appropriate atomic orbitals (s, p and d) of the metal hybridise to give a set of equivalent orbitals of definite geometry such as square planar, tetrahedral, octahedral and so on. A strong covalent bond is formed only when the orbitals overlap to the maximum extent. The d-orbitals involved in the hybridisation may be either inner d-orbitals i.e. $(n-1)$ d or outer d-orbitals i.e. nd. The complexes formed are called inner orbital complex (low spin complex) and outer orbital complex (high spin complex) respectively. Further, the complexes can be paramagnetic or diamagnetic in nature. The drawbacks of this theory are that this involves number of assumptions and also does not explain the colour of the complex. Answer the following questions : (a) Predict whether $[CoF_6]^{3-}$ is diamagnetic or paramagnetic and why ? [Atomic number : Co $= 27$] (b) What is the coordination number of Co in $[Co(en)_2Cl_2]^+$ ? (c) (i) Write the IUPAC name of the given complex : $[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]^{2+}$. (ii) Explain $[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}$ is an inner orbital or outer orbital complex. OR (c) Using valence bond theory, deduce the shape and hybridisation of $[Ni(NH_3)_6]^{2+}$ [Atomic number of Ni $= 28$].

answer.text:
(a) $[CoF_6]^{3-}$ is paramagnetic because $F^-$ (a weak-field ligand) does not cause pairing of the electrons, so unpaired electrons remain.
(b) Coordination number = 6.
(c)(i) Diamminedichloridoplatinum(II).
(ii) It uses inner d-orbitals because $NH_3$ (a strong-field ligand) causes pairing of the electrons (an inner-orbital / low-spin complex).
OR (c) In $[Ni(NH_3)_6]^{2+}$, $Ni^{2+}$ is $3d^8$; $NH_3$ does not pair the two unpaired 3d electrons, so the outer 4d orbitals are used. Shape: octahedral; hybridisation: $sp^3d^2$ (an outer-orbital / high-spin complex).

questions.text: The oxidation number of the central atom in a complex is defined as the charge it would carry if all the ligands are removed along with the electron pairs that are shared with the central atom. Similarly the charge on the complex is the sum of the charges of the constituent parts i.e. the sum of the charges on the central metal ion and its surrounding ligands. Based on this, the complex is called neutral if the sum of the charges of the constituents is equal to zero. However, for an anion or cationic complex, the sum of the charges of the constituents is equal to the charge on the coordination sphere. Based on the information, answer the following questions : (a) Define ambidentate ligand with an example. (b) What type of isomerism is shown by $[Co(NH_3)_5Cl]SO_4$ and $[Co(NH_3)_5SO_4]Cl$ ? (c) Define Chelate effect. How it affects the stability of complex ? OR (c) Find the coordination number and oxidation state of chromium in $Na_3[Cr(C_2O_4)_3]$.

answer.text:
(a) An ambidentate ligand is a ligand that has two different donor atoms, either of which can ligate to the metal in the complex. Examples: $NO_2^-$ / $SCN^-$ / $CN^-$ (any one).
(b) Ionisation isomerism.
(c) Chelation: when a bidentate or polydentate ligand ligates to the metal atom/ion, forming a ring (a chelate). The more the chelation, the greater the stability (the chelate effect).
OR (c) Coordination number = 6; oxidation state of the metal = +3.

questions.text: (i) Give reasons : (I) $[Ni(CO)_4]$ is diamagnetic whereas $[NiCl_4]^{2-}$ is paramagnetic. [Atomic number : Ni $= 28$] (II) CO is a stronger complexing agent than $NH_3$. (III) The trans isomer of complex $[Co(en)_2Cl_2]^+$ is optically inactive. (ii) Using Crystal Field theory, write the number of unpaired electrons in octahedral complexes of $Fe^{3+}$ in the presence of : (I) Strong field ligand (II) Weak field ligand. [Atomic number : Fe $= 26$]

answer.text:
(a)(i)(I) In $[Ni(CO)_4]$, CO (a strong-field ligand) causes pairing of the electrons, so there is no unpaired electron (diamagnetic); whereas $Cl^-$ (a weak-field ligand) does not cause pairing, so unpaired electrons are present (paramagnetic).
(II) CO can form both a sigma ($\sigma$) and a pi ($\pi$) bond with the central metal atom; the metal-to-ligand back-bonding creates a synergic effect between CO and the metal.
(III) The mirror images are superimposable / there is a plane of symmetry (so the complex is optically inactive).

questions.text: (i) Name the type of isomerism exhibited by the following compounds. Also draw their corresponding isomers. (III) Geometrical (cis–trans) isomerism.

questions.text: (a) What is meant by crystal field splitting energy ? For a $d^4$ ion, write the configuration if (i) $\Delta_o < P$, and (ii) $\Delta_o > P$. (b) Explain why in tetrahedral coordination entities, low spin configurations are rarely observed.

answer.text:
(a) The crystal field splitting energy ($\Delta_o$) is the difference of energy between the two sets of d-orbitals ($t_{2g}$ and $e_g$) that arises due to the presence of ligands in a definite geometry (i.e. the energy required to split the degenerate d-orbitals into these two sets).
(i) $t_{2g}^{3}\,e_g^{1}$
(ii) $t_{2g}^{4}\,e_g^{0}$
(b) In the second case the orbital splitting energy is not sufficiently large to cause pairing of electrons, so the configuration remains high-spin.

questions.text: Werner's coordination theory in 1893 was the first attempt to explain the bonding in coordination complexes. It must be remembered that this theory was put forward before the electron had been discovered by J.J. Thomson in 1897, and before the electronic theory of valency. Werner was able to explain the nature of bonding in complexes and he concluded that in complexes, the metal shows two different sorts of valency : primary and secondary. Primary valences are normally ionisable whereas secondary valences are non ionisable. (a) One mole of $CrCl_3 \cdot 4H_2O$ precipitates one mole of AgCl when treated with excess of $AgNO_3$ solution. OR (c) (ii) Write two differences between primary and secondary valences in coordination compounds.

answer.text:
(a)(i) The complex is $[Cr(H_2O)_4Cl_2]Cl$.
(ii) Its coordination number is 6.
(b) Double salts dissociate into their constituent simple ions when dissolved in water, whereas complex (coordination) compounds do not dissociate completely into their ions in solution (or any other suitable difference).
(c)(i) Increasing order of molar conductivity (number of ions):
$[Cr(NH_3)_3Cl_3] < [Cr(NH_3)_5Cl]Cl_2 < [Cr(NH_3)_6]Cl_3$.
OR (c)(ii) Difference between primary and secondary valency (any two):

questions.text: The Crystal Field Theory (CFT) of coordination compounds is based on the effect of different crystal fields (provided by the ligands taken as point charges) on the degeneracy of d-orbital energies of the central metal atom/ion. The splitting of the d-orbitals provides different electronic arrangements in strong and weak crystal fields. In tetrahedral coordination entity formation, the d-orbital splitting is smaller as compared to the octahedral entity. (a) On the basis of CFT, explain why $[Ti(H_2O)_6]Cl_3$ complex is coloured ? What happens on heating the complex $[Ti(H_2O)_6]Cl_3$ ? Give reason. [Atomic no. : Ti $= 22$] (b) (i) What is crystal field splitting energy ? OR (b) (ii) On the basis of $\Delta_o$ and P (pairing energy), how can you differentiate between a strong field ligand and a weak field ligand ? (c) Why are low spin tetrahedral complexes rarely observed ?

answer.text:
(a) (The complex is coloured) due to the presence of one unpaired electron in the $t_{2g}$ level, which gets excited to the $e_g$ level ($t_{2g}^1 \to e_g^1$, a d–d transition). When heated, the water ligand is lost, so crystal-field splitting no longer occurs and it becomes colourless.
(b) Crystal-field splitting energy: the energy required to split the degenerate d-orbitals into two sets ($t_{2g}$ and $e_g$) due to the presence of ligands in a definite geometry.
(c) Because the orbital-splitting energies are not sufficiently large to force pairing / due to the low crystal-field splitting energy.
OR (b)(ii) $\Delta_o < P$: a weak-field ligand (no pairing). $\Delta_o > P$: a strong-field ligand (pairing occurs).

questions.text: The Valence Bond Theory (VBT) explains the formation, magnetic behaviour and geometry of coordination compounds. The Crystal Field Theory (CFT) of coordination compounds is based on the effect of different crystal fields (provided by the ligands taken as point charges), on the degeneracy of d-orbital energies of the central metal atom/ion. The splitting of the d-orbitals provides different electronic arrangements in strong and weak crystal fields. (a) In octahedral crystal field, energies of which d-orbitals will be raised when ligands approach the central metal atom/ion ? Give reason in support of your answer. (b) Using crystal field theory, write the electronic configuration of central metal atom/ion of the following : (i) $[CoF_6]^{3-}$ (ii) $[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}$ [At. No. : Co $= 27$] (c) $[NiCl_4]^{2-}$ is paramagnetic while $[Ni(CO)_4]$ is diamagnetic though both are tetrahedral. Why ? [Atomic No. : Ni $= 28$] OR (c) Write hybridization and magnetic behaviour of the complex $[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}$. [Atomic No. : Fe $= 26$]
questions.topic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

answer.text:
(a) The two d-orbitals that point along the axes are $d_{x^2-y^2}$ and $d_{z^2}$. In an octahedral crystal field the ligands approach the metal atom/ion along the axes, so these two orbitals ($e_g$) experience greater repulsion and are raised in energy.
(b)(i) $[CoF_6]^{3-}$: $Co^{3+} = 3d^6$; $F^-$ is a weak-field ligand, so high-spin $t_{2g}^{4}\,e_g^{2}$.
(ii) $[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}$: $Co^{3+} = 3d^6$; $NH_3$ is a stronger field ligand, so low-spin $t_{2g}^{6}\,e_g^{0}$.
(c) In $[NiCl_4]^{2-}$, $Cl^-$ is a weak-field ligand and does not pair up the unpaired 3d electrons, so it is paramagnetic (tetrahedral, $sp^3$). In $[Ni(CO)_4]$, CO is a strong-field ligand and pairs up the electrons, so it is diamagnetic.
OR (c) For $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$: hybridisation $dsp^2$, square planar, diamagnetic; whereas $[NiCl_4]^{2-}$ has $sp^3$ hybridisation and is paramagnetic.

questions.text: Account for the following : (a) Benzyl chloride is highly reactive towards $S_N1$ reaction. (b) ($\pm$)-Butan-2-ol is optically inactive, though it contains a chiral carbon atom. (c) Chloroform is stored in closed dark coloured bottles.

(b) Because the product is a racemic mixture — an equimolar mixture of the two enantiomers of butan-2-ol (so it is optically inactive).
(c) Chloroform is stored in dark, closed bottles filled to the brim because it forms the poisonous gas phosgene ($COCl_2$) in the presence of air and light.

questions.text: Why is boiling point of o-dichlorobenzene higher than p-dichlorobenzene but melting point of para isomer is higher than ortho isomer ?

answer.text:
(a) The boiling point of the ortho isomer is higher because it has a higher dipole moment (greater polarity) and stronger intermolecular interactions.
(b) The melting point of the para isomer is higher because it is symmetric and fits better into the crystal lattice.

questions.text: Nucleophilic Substitution reaction of haloalkane can be conducted according to both $S_N1$ and $S_N2$ mechanisms. $S_N1$ is a two step reaction while $S_N2$ is a single step reaction. For any haloalkane which mechanism is followed depends on factors such as structure of haloalkane, properties of leaving group, nucleophilic reagent and solvent. In $S_N1$ reaction, the polarity of the system increases from the reactant to the transition state, because a polar solvent has a greater effect on the transition state than the reactant, thereby reducing activation energy and accelerating the reaction. In $S_N2$ reaction, the polarity of the system generally does not change from the reactant to the transition state and only charge dispersion occurs. Generally weak polar solvent is favourable for $S_N2$ reaction, while strong polar solvent is favourable for $S_N1$. Answer the following questions : (a) Why racemisation occurs in $S_N1$ ? (b) Why is ethanol less polar than water ? (c) Which one of the following in each pair is more reactive towards $S_N2$ reaction ? (i) $CH_3{-}CH_2{-}I$ or $CH_3CH_2{-}Cl$ (ii) $C_6H_{11}{-}Cl$ (cyclohexyl chloride) or $C_6H_{11}{-}CH_2{-}Cl$ (cyclohexylmethyl chloride) OR (c) Arrange the following in the increasing order of their reactivity towards $S_N1$ reactions : (i) 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane, 1-Bromopentane, 2-Bromopentane (ii) 1-Bromo-3-methylbutane, 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane, 2-Bromo-3-methylbutane

answer.text:
(a) A tertiary halide undergoes $S_N1$ readily because of the formation of a stable planar ($sp^2$-hybridised) carbocation.
(b) Ethanol is a weaker acid than water due to the +I effect (electron-releasing nature) of the ethyl group.
(c)(i) $CH_3CH_2I$ (iodoethane).
(ii) Benzyl chloride, $C_6H_5{-}CH_2{-}Cl$.
OR (c)(i) Increasing order of reactivity towards $S_N1$: 1-bromopentane < 2-bromopentane < 2-bromo-2-methylbutane.
(ii) Increasing order of reactivity towards $S_N1$: 1-bromo-3-methylbutane < 2-bromo-3-methylbutane < 2-bromo-2-methylbutane.

questions.text: Give reasons for the following : (i) Grignard reagent should be prepared under anhydrous conditions. (ii) Alkyl halides give alcohol with aqueous KOH whereas in the presence of alcoholic KOH, alkenes are formed.

questions.text: (a) Which of the following is an allylic halide ? questions.text: Give reasons for the following : (a) Chlorine is ortho/para directing in electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions, though chlorine is an electron withdrawing group. (b) Racemic mixture is optically inactive. (c) Allyl chloride is hydrolysed more readily than n-propyl chloride.

answer.text:

(b) Because the mixture contains two enantiomers in equal proportions, giving zero optical rotation (external compensation of equal amounts of the (+) and (–) forms).

questions.text: (a) What type of nucleophilic substitution ($S_N1$ or $S_N2$) occurs in the hydrolysis of 2-Bromobutane to form ($\pm$)-Butan-2-ol ? Give reason. (b) What happens when chlorobenzene and methyl chloride are treated with sodium metal in dry ether ?

questions.text: Account for the following : (a) Haloalkanes react with AgCN to form isocyanide as main product. (b) Allyl chloride shows high reactivity towards $S_N1$ reaction. (c) Haloarenes are extremely less reactive towards nucleophilic substitution reactions.

answer.text:

questions.text: Account for the following : (a) The C $-$ Cl bond length in chlorobenzene is shorter than that in methyl chloride. (b) Grignard reagents should be prepared under anhydrous conditions. (c) In case of optically active alkyl halides, $S_N1$ reactions are accompanied by racemisation.

answer.text:
(a) In chlorobenzene there is resonance, which gives the C--Cl bond a partial double-bond character; the carbon bonded to Cl is $sp^2$ hybridised, giving a shorter C--Cl bond than in $CH_3Cl$, where the carbon is $sp^3$ hybridised. Hence chlorobenzene is less reactive.
(b) The Grignard reagent reacts with water to form the corresponding hydrocarbon, so it must be prepared and handled under anhydrous conditions.
(c) In an $S_N1$ reaction a planar carbocation is formed as an intermediate, and the nucleophile may attack from either side of this planar carbocation, giving a racemic mixture.

questions.text: Why are haloarenes less reactive towards nucleophilic substitution reaction ? Give two reasons.

questions.text: Give reasons for the following : (a) Although chlorine is an electron-withdrawing group, yet it is ortho-, para-directing in electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions. questions.text: (i) Write the mechanism of the following reaction : $2CH_3CH_2OH \xrightarrow[\;413\ K\;]{\;H^+\;} CH_3{-}CH_2{-}O{-}CH_2{-}CH_3 + H_2O$ (ii) Why ortho-nitrophenol is steam volatile while para-nitrophenol is not ?

$C_2H_5OH + H^+ \rightarrow C_2H_5\overset{+}{O}H_2$; then $C_2H_5OH + C_2H_5\overset{+}{O}H_2 \rightarrow C_2H_5{-}\overset{+}{O}H{-}C_2H_5 + H_2O \rightarrow C_2H_5{-}O{-}C_2H_5 + H^+$.

questions.text: (a) Write the mechanism of the following reaction : $CH_3{-}CH_2{-}OH \xrightarrow[\;443\ K\;]{\;H^+\;} CH_2{=}CH_2 + H_2O$ (b) Write the equation of the reaction for the preparation of phenol from cumene.

questions.text: Explain the mechanism of acid catalysed hydration of ethene.

answer.text:
Acid-catalysed hydration of an alkene to an alcohol proceeds through three steps:
Step 1 — Protonation of the alkene to form a carbocation by electrophilic attack of $H_3O^+$ (formed by $H_2O + H^+ \rightarrow H_3O^+$).
Step 2 — Nucleophilic attack of water on the carbocation to give a protonated alcohol (an oxonium ion).

questions.text: Alcohols and Phenols are acidic in nature. Electron withdrawing groups in phenol increase its acidic strength and electron releasing groups decrease it. Alcohols undergo nucleophilic substitution with hydrogen halides to yield alkyl halides. Dehydration of alcohols gives alkenes. On oxidation, primary alcohols yield aldehydes with mild oxidising agents and carboxylic acids with strong oxidising agents, while secondary alcohols yield ketones. Tertiary alcohols are resistant to oxidation. The presence of $-$ OH group in phenols activates the aromatic ring towards electrophilic substitution and directs the incoming group to ortho and para positions due to resonance effect. (a) Write the mechanism of acid dehydration of ethanol to yield ethene. (b) (i) Why are tertiary alcohols resistant to oxidation ? OR (b) (ii) Write the structure of the major product expected from the dinitration of 3-methylphenol. (c) Why is ortho-nitrophenol more acidic than ortho-methoxyphenol ?

answer.text:
(a) Acid-catalysed dehydration of ethanol to ethene proceeds in three steps:
Step 1 — Protonation of the alcohol by $H^+$ to form the protonated alcohol (oxonium ion);
Step 2 — Loss of water from the protonated alcohol to form a carbocation;
Step 3 — Deprotonation of the carbocation (loss of an adjacent $H^+$) to form the alkene ($CH_2{=}CH_2$) and regenerate $H^+$.
(b)(i) It does not undergo the aldol condensation because of the absence of an $\alpha$-hydrogen atom.
OR (b)(ii) The product is 4-methyl-2-nitrophenol (a nitration product of p-cresol).
(c) The $-NO_2$ group is electron-withdrawing and increases the stability of the phenoxide ion (raising acidity), whereas the $-OCH_3$ group is electron-donating and decreases the stability of the phenoxide ion (lowering acidity).

questions.text: Ethers are prepared by the dehydration of alcohols in presence of protic acids at 413 K. Symmetrical and unsymmetrical ethers can also be prepared by Williamson synthesis. This reaction involves $S_N2$ attack of an alkoxide ion on primary alkyl halide. If a tertiary alkyl halide is used, elimination reaction occurs and an alkene is formed, no ether is formed. C $-$ O bond in ethers are cleaved under drastic conditions with excess of HI. When unsymmetrical ethers react with HI, the alkyl halide is formed from smaller alkyl group. If one of the alkyl group is tertiary, the alkyl halide is formed from the tertiary alkyl group because tertiary alkyl carbocation is more stable than the primary carbocation. Cleavage of alkyl aryl ethers takes place at the alkyl-oxygen bond due to more stable aryl-oxygen bond. The order of reactivity of hydrogen halides is HI $>$ HBr $>$ HCl. Aromatic ethers undergo electrophilic substitution reactions. The alkoxy group attached to the aromatic ring activates the ring towards electrophilic substitution and directs the incoming group to ortho- and para-positions. (a) Complete the following equations : (i) $C_6H_5OCH_3 + CH_3Cl \xrightarrow[\;CS_2\;]{\;\text{Anhyd. }AlCl_3\;}$ (ii) $C_6H_5OCH_3 \xrightarrow{\;\text{Conc. }(HNO_3 + H_2SO_4)\;}$ (b) (i) Write the names of alkyl halide and sodium alkoxide used to prepare tert-butyl ethyl ether. OR (b) (ii) Anisole on reaction with HI gives phenol and $CH_3{-}I$ and not methanol and iodobenzene. Justify the statement. (c) Why is C $-$ O $-$ C bond angle in ethers slightly greater than tetrahedral angle ?

answer.text:
(a)(i) Anisole undergoes Friedel--Crafts methylation ($CH_3Cl$/anhyd. $AlCl_3$) to give o- and p-methylanisole (mainly the p-isomer).
(ii) On nitration, anisole gives o- and p-nitroanisole (mainly the p-isomer).
(b)(i) Ethyl tert-butyl ether is best prepared by Williamson synthesis from an ethyl halide and sodium tert-butoxide: $C_2H_5X$ and $(CH_3)_3C{-}O{-}Na$.
OR (b)(ii) In anisole the $O{-}C_6H_5$ bond is stronger than the $O{-}CH_3$ bond because of resonance (the $sp^2$ carbon gives the $O{-}C_6H_5$ bond a partial double-bond character), so cleavage by HBr occurs at the $O{-}CH_3$ bond.
(c) Di-tert-butyl ether cannot be made by Williamson synthesis because of the steric repulsion between the two bulky tert-butyl groups (elimination occurs instead).

questions.text: Explain why : (i) Carboxyl group in benzoic acid is meta directing. (ii) Sodium bisulphite is used for the purification of aldehydes and ketones. (iii) Carboxylic acids do not give characteristic reactions of carbonyl group.

answer.text:

(ii) Aldehydes and ketones form crystalline addition (bisulphite) compounds with $NaHSO_3$, which on hydrolysis regenerate the pure aldehyde or ketone — used for purification.

(d) Why are $\alpha$-hydrogen atoms of aldehydes and ketones acidic in nature ? (e) Write a chemical test to distinguish between Benzaldehyde and Benzoic acid.

answer.text:

questions.text: (i) Write the reaction involved in Cannizzaro's reaction. (ii) Why is the boiling point of aldehydes and ketones lower than that of corresponding carboxylic acids ? (iii) An organic compound 'A' with molecular formula $C_5H_8O_2$ is reduced to n-pentane with hydrazine followed by heating with NaOH and Glycol. 'A' forms a dioxime with hydroxylamine and gives a positive Iodoform and Tollen's test. Identify 'A' and give its reaction for Iodoform and Tollen's test.

answer.text:
(a)(i) Cannizzaro reaction of methanal (formaldehyde) with conc. KOH gives methanol and potassium formate:
$2\,HCHO \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{conc. }KOH} CH_3OH + HCOOK$.
(ii) Carboxylic acids have higher boiling points than aldehydes/ketones because they have strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding, whereas aldehydes and ketones have only weak dipole–dipole interactions.
(iii) $A = $ 4-oxopentanal, $CH_3{-}CO{-}CH_2{-}CH_2{-}CHO$.
It gives a positive iodoform test (yellow ppt of $CHI_3$) with $NaOH + I_2$ (due to the $CH_3CO-$ group), and its $-CHO$ group is oxidised by Tollens' reagent to the carboxylate with a silver mirror:
$CH_3CO{-}CH_2CH_2{-}CHO \xrightarrow[\text{warm}]{[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+,\ OH^-} CH_3CO{-}CH_2{-}CH_2{-}COO^- + Ag\downarrow$.

questions.text: (i) Account for the following : (1) Oxidation of aldehydes is easier as compared to ketones. (2) The alpha ($\alpha$) hydrogen atoms of aldehydes are acidic in nature. questions.text: Write the stepwise mechanism of nucleophilic addition reactions in the carbonyl compounds.

questions.text: Explain the following reactions and write chemical equation involved : (a) Wolff-Kishner reduction (b) Etard reaction (c) Cannizzaro reaction

answer.text:
(A)(a) Wolff–Kishner reduction: the carbonyl group of an aldehyde/ketone is reduced to a $-CH_2-$ group on treatment with hydrazine, followed by heating with NaOH/KOH in a high-boiling solvent (ethylene glycol):
$>C{=}O \xrightarrow[-H_2O]{NH_2NH_2} >C{=}NNH_2 \xrightarrow[\text{heat}]{KOH/\text{ethylene glycol}} >CH_2 + N_2$.
(b) Étard reaction: chromyl chloride oxidises the methyl group of toluene to a chromium complex, which on hydrolysis gives benzaldehyde: $C_6H_5CH_3 \xrightarrow[\;2.\ H_3O^+,\ \Delta\;]{\;1.\ CrO_2Cl_2,\ CS_2\;} C_6H_5CHO$.
(c) Cannizzaro reaction: an aldehyde with no $\alpha$-hydrogen, on heating with conc. alkali, undergoes disproportionation to give the salt of a carboxylic acid and an alcohol: $2\,C_6H_5CHO \xrightarrow{\text{conc. }NaOH} C_6H_5CH_2OH + C_6H_5COONa$.

NaOH}\;} B \xrightarrow{\;\Delta\;} C$

questions.text: (a) How can acetaldehyde be prepared from acetyl chloride ? (b) Propanal is more reactive than propanone towards nucleophilic addition reaction. Give reason.

answer.text:
(a) Acetaldehyde is prepared by the Rosenmund reduction, in which acetyl chloride is hydrogenated over the poisoned catalyst palladium on barium sulphate:
$CH_3COCl \xrightarrow[\text{Pd--BaSO}_4]{H_2} CH_3CHO$.
(b) Propanal is more reactive than propanone towards nucleophilic addition. This is because of the lesser steric hindrance and the greater electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon in propanal (an aldehyde) than in propanone (a ketone, which has two electron-releasing alkyl groups and greater steric crowding).

questions.text: An organic compound 'A' (molecular formula $C_8H_8O$) gives 2,4-DNP test. It does not give Tollen's test, but gives a yellow precipitate 'B' with NaOH and $I_2$. Acetophenone with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine gives the corresponding 2,4-DNP derivative; with $I_2$/NaOH it gives the iodoform test (yellow $CHI_3$, $B$, and sodium benzoate); and on oxidation with $KMnO_4/H^+$ it gives benzoic acid ($C$).

NaOH}\;} C + C_6H_5COONa$. (ii) Give reasons for the following : (I) Carboxylic acids do not give the characteristic reactions of carbonyl group. (II) Ethanoic acid is a stronger acid than ethanol.

questions.text: Give reasons for the following : (a) Benzoic acid does not undergo Friedel-Crafts reaction. (b) HCHO is more reactive than $CH_3CHO$ towards addition of HCN. (c) Vinyl group directly attached with carboxylic acid should decrease the acidity of corresponding carboxylic acid due to resonance, but on the contrary it increases the acidity.

answer.text:
(a) Because the carboxyl group is deactivating, and the catalyst aluminium chloride (a Lewis acid) gets bonded to the carboxyl group (forms a salt) — so a carboxylic acid does not undergo the Friedel–Crafts reaction.
(b) Because the carbonyl carbon of HCHO is more electrophilic than that of $CH_3CHO$ / due to the +I effect and the steric effect of the methyl group, $CH_3CHO$ is less reactive.
(c) Because of the greater electronegativity of the $sp^2$-hybridised carbon to which the carboxyl carbon is attached.

questions.text: Give reasons for the following : (a) Carboxylic acids have higher boiling point than alcohols of comparable molecular masses. (b) Alpha ($\alpha$) hydrogens of aldehydes and ketones are acidic in nature. (c) Nucleophilic addition of ammonia and its derivatives does not occur with carbonyl group in strongly acidic medium.
questions.topic: Nomenclature and Structure of Carbonyl Group

answer.text:
(a) Carboxylic acids have high boiling points because of the extensive association of their molecules through intermolecular hydrogen bonding (dimer formation).
(b) They are more acidic (than phenols/alcohols) because of the strong electron-withdrawing effect of the carbonyl group and the resonance stabilisation of their conjugate base (the carboxylate ion).
(c) The reaction is carried out in a strongly acidic medium because protonation of the nucleophile takes place there, reducing its nucleophilicity (so a strongly acidic medium is avoided for such additions).

questions.text: Write the reaction involved in (a) Rosenmund's reduction (b) Cannizzaro's reaction (c) Hell $-$ Volhard $-$ Zelinsky reaction

answer.text:
(a) Rosenmund reduction — benzoyl chloride is hydrogenated over Pd-BaSO$_4$ to benzaldehyde:
$C_6H_5COCl \xrightarrow[\text{Pd-BaSO}_4]{H_2} C_6H_5CHO$.
(b) Cannizzaro reaction — methanal with concentrated KOH disproportionates:
$2HCHO + \text{conc. }KOH \xrightarrow{\Delta} CH_3OH + HCOOK$.
(c) Hell--Volhard--Zelinsky reaction — propanoic acid with (i) $Cl_2$/red P, then (ii) $H_2O$, gives 2-chloropropanoic acid:
$CH_3CH_2COOH \xrightarrow[(ii)\,H_2O]{(i)\,Cl_2/\text{Red P}} CH_3{-}CHCl{-}COOH$ (or any other correct reaction).

questions.text: (a) How will you convert the following : (i) Propanone to Propene (ii) Benzoic acid to Benzaldehyde (iii) Benzene to m-Nitroacetophenone (b) (i) Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of their reactivity towards HCN : $(CH_3)_2C{=}O$, $((CH_3)_3C)_2C{=}O$, $CH_3CH{=}O$ (ii) Identify the compounds, which would undergo Aldol condensation : HCHO, $C_6H_5CHO$, $CH_3CHO$

questions.text: (a) Give chemical tests to distinguish between the following pairs of compounds : (i) Acetophenone and Benzophenone (ii) Propanal and Propanone (iii) Pentan$-$2$-$one and Pentan$-$3$-$one (b) (i) Which of the following acids is stronger and why ? $CH_2FCOOH$, $CH_3COOH$ (ii) Arrange the following compounds in the increasing order of their boiling points : $CH_3OCH_3$, $CH_3CH_2CH_3$, $CH_3CH_2OH$, $CH_3CHO$

questions.text: What happens when : (a) Propanenitrile is treated with phenyl magnesium bromide followed by hydrolysis ? (b) p-fluorotoluene is treated with $CrO_3$ in the presence of acetic anhydride followed by hydrolysis with aqueous acid. (c) Phthalic acid is treated with $NH_3$ followed by heating ? Write chemical reactions in support of your answer.

answer.text:
(a) The nitrile reacts with the Grignard reagent and, on acidic hydrolysis, gives a ketone (1-phenylpropan-1-one):
$CH_3{-}CH_2{-}C{\equiv}N + C_6H_5MgBr \xrightarrow[H_3O^+]{\text{ether}} C_2H_5{-}CO{-}C_6H_5$.

questions.text: Living systems are made up of various complex biomolecules like carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, etc. Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones or molecules which provide such units on hydrolysis. They are broadly classified into three groups — monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides. Monosaccharides are held together by glycosidic linkages to form disaccharides like sucrose, maltose or polysaccharides like starch and cellulose. Another biomolecule : proteins are polymers of $\alpha$-amino acids which are linked by peptide bonds. Ten amino acids are called essential amino acids. Structure and shape of proteins can be studied at four different levels i.e. primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary, each level being more complex than the previous one. Answer the following questions : (i) What is the difference between a glycosidic linkage and peptide linkage ? (ii) Which amino acids are called essential amino acids ? (iii) What are the common types of secondary structures of proteins ? Write any two forces which stabilise the secondary and tertiary structures of protein. OR (iii) Define denaturation of protein with an example. During denaturation which structures of protein lose their biological activity ?

answer.text:
(i) Peptide linkage: the $-CO{-}NH-$ linkage formed when two amino acids are joined. Glycosidic linkage: the linkage formed when two monosaccharides are joined through an oxygen atom.
(ii) Essential amino acids: those which are not synthesised in the body and must be obtained through the diet.
(iii) The two secondary structures of proteins are the $\alpha$-helix and the $\beta$-pleated sheet; they are stabilised by (any two): hydrogen bonds, van der Waals forces, disulphide linkages, electrostatic forces of attraction.
OR (iii) Denaturation: the loss of biological activity when the native form of a protein is subjected to a change in temperature, pH, etc. (e.g. the curdling of milk). During denaturation the secondary and tertiary structures are lost, so the protein loses its biological activity.

questions.text: Carbohydrates are essential for life in both plants and animals. Carbohydrates are used as storage molecules as starch in plants and glycogen in animals. Structure and shape of proteins can be studied at four different levels i.e., primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary, each level being more complex than the previous one. The secondary or tertiary structure of proteins get disturbed on change of pH or temperature and they are not able to perform their functions. This is called denaturation of proteins. questions.text: Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones that represent enormous structural diversity in terms of the arrangement of atoms in space, resulting in hundreds of stereoisomers. Although the chemical properties of most stereoisomers may not be very different, their metabolic rate and utilization in biological systems is significantly different and known to influence the overall carbohydrate metabolism. Structural variants, which arise due to a different arrangement of atoms in three-dimensional space are known as stereoisomers. The number of stereoisomers can be theoretically estimated by using the formula $2^n$, where 'n' is the number of stereocenters or asymmetric (chiral) carbon atoms in a molecule. Out of these stereoisomers, there are some structures, which are mirror images of each other, and they are referred to as enantiomers. (a) Give chemical reactions to show the presence of an aldehydic group and straight chain in glucose. (b) (i) Define anomers. OR (b) (ii) Draw the structure of $\alpha$-D-Glucopyranose. (c) Sucrose is known as invert sugar. Explain.

answer.text:
(a) Glucose on oxidation with bromine water gives gluconic acid:
$CHO{-}(CHOH)_4{-}CH_2OH \xrightarrow{Br_2\text{ water}} COOH{-}(CHOH)_4{-}CH_2OH$.
On prolonged heating with HI, glucose is reduced to n-hexane:
$CHO{-}(CHOH)_4{-}CH_2OH \xrightarrow{HI,\ \Delta} CH_3{-}CH_2{-}CH_2{-}CH_2{-}CH_2{-}CH_3$.
(b)(i) The two cyclic structures of glucose differ only in the configuration of the $-OH$ group at $C_1$; such isomers are called anomers.
OR Stereoisomers which differ in the configuration of the $-OH$ group at $C_1$ or $C_2$ are called epimers.
(b)(ii) The cyclic structure is that of $\beta$-D-(+)-glucopyranose (a six-membered pyranose ring with the anomeric $-OH$ at $C_1$ in the equatorial / $\beta$ position).
(c) Hydrolysis of dextrorotatory sucrose brings about a change in the sign of rotation, inverting the optical rotation from dextro to laevo; the product of hydrolysis is therefore called invert sugar.

answer.text:

questions.text: The $\alpha$-amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. All $\alpha$-amino acids exist as zwitter ion due to which they show amphoteric behaviour. All amino acids are joined through peptide bond. Proteins are broadly classified as globular proteins and fibrous proteins. Globular proteins are water soluble, whereas fibrous proteins are not. The complete structure of protein is discussed at four different levels i.e. primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structures. Protein loses its biological activity in denatured form. (c) (i) How can you differentiate between Fibrous protein and Globular protein ? OR (c) (ii) Write the names of two different secondary structures of proteins.

answer.text:
(a)(i) Peptide linkage: a linkage that joins amino acids through a $-CO{-}NH-$ bond.
(ii) When a protein in its native form is subjected to a physical change (temperature) or a chemical change (pH), it loses its biological activity (denaturation).
(b) Due to zwitterion formation, which can react with both acids and bases (because of the presence of both a carboxylic and an amino group).
(c)(i) Fibrous protein: parallel polypeptide-chain structure / insoluble in water. Globular protein: spherical polypeptide-chain structure / soluble in water (any one difference).
OR (c)(ii) The two common secondary structures of proteins are the $\alpha$-helix and the $\beta$-pleated sheet.

questions.text: Differentiate between the following : (i) Peptide linkage and Glycosidic linkage (ii) Essential amino acids and Non-essential amino acids

answer.text:

questions.text: Write the reactions of D-Glucose with the following : (a) HI (b) $Br_2$ water (c) Conc. $HNO_3$

answer.text:
(a) On prolonged heating with HI, glucose is reduced to n-hexane:
$CHO{-}(CHOH)_4{-}CH_2OH \xrightarrow{HI,\ \Delta} CH_3{-}(CH_2)_4{-}CH_3$.
(b) With bromine water, glucose is oxidised to the six-carbon gluconic acid:
$CHO{-}(CHOH)_4{-}CH_2OH \xrightarrow{Br_2\text{ water}} COOH{-}(CHOH)_4{-}CH_2OH$.
(c) With concentrated $HNO_3$, glucose is oxidised at both ends to the dicarboxylic saccharic (glucaric) acid:
$CHO{-}(CHOH)_4{-}CH_2OH \xrightarrow{\text{conc. }HNO_3} COOH{-}(CHOH)_4{-}COOH$.

questions.text: Living systems are made up of various complex biomolecules like carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, etc. Proteins and carbohydrates are essential constituents of our food. Proteins can be classified into two types on the basis of their molecular shape — Fibrous and Globular proteins. Vitamins are accessory food factors required in the diet. They are classified as fat-soluble and water-soluble. Deficiency of vitamins leads to many diseases. (a) The building blocks of proteins are $\alpha$-amino acids; those of nucleic acids are nucleotides. Fibrous proteins: the polypeptide chains run parallel and are held together by hydrogen and disulphide bonds, giving a fibre-like structure; globular proteins: the polypeptide chains coil around to give a spherical shape (or any other correct difference).

questions.text: Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones or the compounds which produce such units on hydrolysis. They have been broadly classified into three groups — monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides. The carbohydrates may also be classified as either reducing or non-reducing sugars. An important monosaccharide glucose is an aldohexose and is correctly named as D(+)-glucose. It was assigned the open structure on the basis of its reactions with HI, $NH_2OH$, $Br_2$ water, $(CH_3CO)_2O$ and nitric acid. Despite having the $-$ CHO group, glucose does not give Schiff's test and hydrogen sulphite addition product with $NaHSO_3$. It was found that glucose forms a six-membered ring in which one of the $-$ OH groups add to the $-$ CHO group and form a cyclic hemiacetal structure. (a) How do you explain the following ? (i) Presence of a carbonyl group in glucose (ii) Presence of five $-$ OH groups in glucose which are attached to different carbon atoms. (b) What type of carbohydrates are called reducing sugars ? (c) (i) In D(+)-glucose, what do the letter 'D' and sign '(+)' represent ? OR (c) (ii) Draw the six-membered ring structure of $\alpha$-D(+)-glucose.

answer.text:
(a)(i) Glucose reacts with hydroxylamine ($H_2N{-}OH$) to form an oxime, and with HCN to form a cyanohydrin — showing the presence of a carbonyl group (or give the correct chemical equation).
(ii) Glucose gives a stable pentaacetate with acetic anhydride $(CH_3CO)_2O$ — showing the presence of five $-OH$ groups (or give the correct chemical equation).
(b) Reducing sugars are those which reduce Tollens' reagent / Fehling's solution.
(c)(i) In D-(+)-glucose, 'D' stands for the configuration (relative to glyceraldehyde) and '(+)' stands for the dextrorotatory nature of the molecule.
OR (c)(ii) The cyclic structure is that of $\beta$-D-glucopyranose (a six-membered pyranose ring with the anomeric $-OH$ at $C_1$ in the $\beta$-position).
